title: U.S. Loses Measles-Free Status After 26 Years; the Outbreak That Cost It Began in West Texas

content:
The United States has lost its measles elimination status after 26 years, the Pan American Health Organization announced Tuesday, Nov. 17 — and the chain of transmission that cost the country the designation began with the West Texas outbreak in early 2025.

PAHO’s verification commission found a single chain of measles transmission that began Jan. 20, 2025, and persisted for more than 12 months, the threshold for re-establishing endemic transmission. The U.S. had held elimination status since 2000. Mexico and Bolivia lost their status the same day.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention counted 5,412 confirmed measles cases in the U.S. through Nov. 12, 2026 — the highest annual total since 1991 and more than double the 2,289 cases recorded in all of 2025. There have been 43 outbreaks this year. The CDC counts six deaths in 2026; a tally of state health department reports by NBC News counts 10.

Across the Americas, PAHO counted 58,213 confirmed cases and 82 deaths as of Nov. 13, compared with 12,806 cases in the same period of 2025. The CDC reports that 96 percent of 2026 U.S. cases were in people who were unvaccinated or whose vaccination status was unknown.

The West Texas connection

The West Texas outbreak began in Gaines County in late January 2025 and spread through close-knit communities with low vaccination coverage. By the time the Texas Department of State Health Services declared the outbreak over on Aug. 18, 2025, it had counted 762 confirmed cases and 99 hospitalizations. Two school-aged children who lived in the outbreak area died; state health officials said neither was vaccinated and neither had known underlying conditions.

Texas has continued to report measles cases in 2026. A DSHS report dated Sept. 16, 2026, listed 192 confirmed cases among Texas residents this year, including 136 among people housed in federal detention facilities in Hudspeth County.

Kindergarten MMR vaccination coverage in the U.S. was 92.4 percent in the 2025-26 school year, down from 95.2 percent in 2019-20, according to the CDC. The 95 percent level is generally considered necessary for herd immunity.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said on social media the administration will work to stop the outbreaks and regain the status. CDC Director Erica Schwartz said, “The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does.”

The designation carries no formal penalties and does not change the federal outbreak response. To regain it, the U.S. must interrupt transmission for at least 12 months; PAHO expects the U.S., Mexico and Bolivia to each submit a plan in the coming weeks. The U.S. retains its elimination status for rubella.

Sources: Associated Press, Nov. 17, 2026; Pan American Health Organization / CDC letter, Nov. 13, 2026; Texas Department of State Health Services, measles data; Hub City Uncovered, Nov. 19, 2026.
